cards.front: What does the slope of a velocity–time graph tell you?
cards.back: The acceleration. (Slope of x–t = velocity; area under v–t = displacement.)

cards.front: Constant acceleration: v = v₀ + {{a·t}}
cards.back: v = v₀ + at. Use it when you do not know the distance.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a v–t line that starts at v₀ and rises. Mark the rise as a·t over a run of t.

cards.front: Constant acceleration: x = x₀ + v₀t + {{½at²}}
cards.back: x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at². Use it when you do not know the final speed.

cards.front: Constant acceleration, no time: v² = v₀² + {{2a(x − x₀)}}
cards.back: v² = v₀² + 2a(x − x₀). Use it when you do not know the time.
cards.sketch_prompt: Sketch a v–t trapezoid and shade the area. Write what the area stands for (distance).

cards.front: Name each part of this velocity–time graph.
cards.back: velocity v; time t; slope = acceleration; area = displacement

cards.front: A ball is thrown straight up. What are its velocity and acceleration at the very top?
cards.back: Velocity = 0, but acceleration is still 9.8 m/s² downward. Gravity never switches off.

cards.front: Match each quantity with its type.
cards.back: Distance and speed are scalars. Displacement and velocity are vectors.

cards.front: You swim the first half of a trip at 2 m/s and the second half at 6 m/s. What is the average speed?
cards.back: 3 m/s, not 4. Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, and you spend more time at the slow speed.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a bar split into two equal halves. Write the time each half takes (d/2 ÷ 2 and d/2 ÷ 6) and add.

cards.front: Newton's second law: F_net = {{m·a}}
cards.back: F_net = ma. Net force (a vector sum) equals mass times acceleration.

cards.front: Kinetic friction: f = {{μN}}
cards.back: f = μN, where N is the normal force (not always mg!) and μ is the friction coefficient.

cards.front: Name the forces and the angle on this incline.
cards.back: angle θ; normal force N; friction f; weight mg

cards.front: A block slides down a smooth incline of angle θ. What is its acceleration?
cards.back: a = g sin θ. The mass cancels, so heavy and light blocks slide the same way.

cards.front: A swimmer pushes the wall with 300 N. What force does the wall put on the swimmer?
cards.back: 300 N in the opposite direction. The two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel each other.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a swimmer and a wall. Draw two arrows of equal length, each starting on a different object.

cards.front: Put the steps for a force problem in order.
cards.back: Draw the object alone, then its forces, then axes, then components, then F_net = ma.
items: Draw every force as an arrow
Write F_net = ma for each axis

cards.front: Match each force with its direction.
cards.back: Normal is perpendicular to the surface; friction is parallel to it.

cards.front: Two masses m₁ > m₂ hang over a light pulley. What is the acceleration?
cards.back: a = (m₁ − m₂)g ÷ (m₁ + m₂). Net weight difference moves the total mass.

cards.front: Kinetic energy: KE = {{½mv²}}
cards.back: KE = ½mv². Double the speed and KE becomes four times bigger.

cards.front: Gravitational potential energy near Earth: PE = {{mgh}}
cards.back: PE = mgh, with h measured from any zero level you choose.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a ball on a shelf and a floor. Mark h and write PE = mgh.

cards.front: Momentum p = {{mv}}. Impulse J = {{FΔt}} = Δp.
cards.back: p = mv (a vector). Impulse equals the change in momentum.

cards.front: In a perfectly inelastic collision, what is conserved: momentum, kinetic energy, or both?
cards.back: Only momentum. Kinetic energy is lost as heat, sound and deformation.

cards.front: Average power: P = {{W/t}} = F·v
cards.back: P = W/t, measured in watts (J/s).

cards.front: Angular momentum: L = {{Iω}}. With no net torque, pulling your arms in makes you spin {{faster}}.
cards.back: L = Iω is conserved. Smaller I means larger ω.

cards.front: Put the steps for a collision problem in order.
cards.back: Define the system, check no outside net force, write p before, write p after, set equal.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a 'before' picture and an 'after' picture with arrows for each velocity.
items: Check there is no outside net force

cards.front: What is the work done by a force F over a displacement d at angle θ?
cards.back: W = F·d·cos θ, in joules. A force at 90° to the motion does no work.

cards.front: Centripetal acceleration: a_c = {{v²/r}}
cards.back: a_c = v²/r, pointing toward the center.

cards.front: Centripetal force: F = {{mv²/r}}, and it points toward the {{center}}.
cards.back: F = mv²/r. It is a name for the net inward force, not a new force.

cards.front: Name the parts of this circular-motion picture.
cards.back: radius r; velocity v; centripetal force; center

cards.front: Torque: τ = {{r·F·sin θ}}
cards.back: τ = rF sin θ, where θ is the angle between the lever arm r and the force F.

cards.front: Rotational form of Newton's second law: τ_net = {{Iα}}
cards.back: τ_net = Iα. Moment of inertia I is the rotational 'mass'.

cards.front: How do you get the speed from the period T of a circle with radius r?
cards.back: v = 2πr/T = 2πrf. One lap is the circumference 2πr, covered in time T.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a circle. Mark one lap as 2πr and label the time for it as T.

cards.front: A solid disk and a ring have the same mass and radius. Which has the larger moment of inertia?
cards.back: The ring (I = MR² vs ½MR²). Mass farther from the axis means more rotational inertia.

cards.front: Is 'centrifugal force' a real force in an inertial frame?
cards.back: No. Objects want to go straight; the inward net force bends the path. The 'outward push' you feel is inertia.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a ball on a string with the string suddenly cut. Show it flying off along the tangent.

cards.front: Hooke's law: F = {{−kx}}
cards.back: F = −kx. The minus sign means the force always points back to equilibrium.

cards.front: Mass on a spring: T = {{2π√(m/k)}}
cards.back: T = 2π√(m/k). A stiffer spring (bigger k) oscillates faster.

cards.front: Simple pendulum (small angle): T = {{2π√(L/g)}}
cards.back: T = 2π√(L/g). Mass and amplitude do not matter.

cards.front: Label this SHM graph.
cards.back: equilibrium x = 0; amplitude A; period T; displacement x

cards.front: Where is the speed of an SHM oscillator largest, and where is its acceleration largest?
cards.back: Speed is largest at equilibrium (x = 0). Acceleration is largest at the extremes (x = ±A).

cards.front: Does the period of a small-angle pendulum depend on its mass or its amplitude?
cards.back: No. Only on the length L and on g.

cards.front: Total energy in SHM: E = {{½kA²}}
cards.back: E = ½kA², constant. It swaps between KE and spring PE.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three bar charts (KE and PE) at x = 0, x = A/2 and x = A. The two bars always add to the same height.

cards.front: Match each SHM word with its meaning.
cards.back: Period is time, frequency is cycles per second, f = 1/T.
pairs: where the net force is zero

cards.front: Newton's law of gravitation: F = {{G·m₁m₂/r²}}
cards.back: F = Gm₁m₂/r², with r measured between the centers.

cards.front: The distance between two masses doubles. What happens to the gravitational force?
cards.back: It becomes four times smaller (inverse-square law).

cards.front: Surface gravity of a planet: g = {{GM/R²}}
cards.back: g = GM/R². The small mass of the object cancels out.

cards.front: Circular orbit speed: v = {{√(GM/r)}}
cards.back: v = √(GM/r). It comes from gravity = centripetal force.

cards.front: Astronauts on the space station float. Is gravity zero up there?
cards.back: No, it is about 90% of its value on the ground. They float because they are in free fall around Earth.

cards.front: Your mass is the same on the Moon. What about your weight?
cards.back: Weight is about 1/6 as big, because the Moon's g is about 1.6 m/s². Mass does not change.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two scales, one on Earth and one on the Moon, with the same person. Write mass and weight on each.

cards.front: Put the steps for an orbit problem in order.
cards.back: Gravity supplies the centripetal force, so GMm/r² = mv²/r, then cancel m and solve.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a satellite on a circle. Draw one arrow toward the planet and label it with both names: gravity and centripetal force.
items: Say gravity is the centripetal force

cards.front: Match each quantity with its value or rule.
cards.back: G and g are different things.

cards.front: Ohm's law: V = {{I·R}}
cards.back: V = IR. Voltage is in volts, current in amperes, resistance in ohms.

cards.front: Electric power: P = {{I·V}} = I²R = {{V²/R}}
cards.back: P = IV. Use I²R when current is known and V²/R when voltage is known.

cards.front: Resistors in series: R_total = {{R₁ + R₂ + …}}
cards.back: In series the resistances add and the current is the same everywhere.

cards.front: Resistors in parallel: 1/R_total = {{1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + …}}
cards.back: In parallel the total is smaller than the smallest resistor. Voltage is the same on each branch.

cards.front: Capacitor: Q = {{C·V}}, and the stored energy is U = {{½CV²}}
cards.back: Q = CV and U = ½CV².

cards.front: Label this series circuit.
cards.back: battery; resistor R₁; resistor R₂; current I

cards.front: Match each connection with its rule.
cards.back: Capacitors behave the opposite way to resistors.

cards.front: Why are the lights and sockets in a home wired in parallel?
cards.back: Each gets the full supply voltage, and if one device fails the others keep working.

cards.front: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
cards.back: If A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other. This makes temperature meaningful.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw three boxes A, B, C. Join A–C and B–C with '=' and write the '=' you can conclude between A and B.

cards.front: First law: ΔU = {{Q − W}} (W is work done by the system)
cards.back: ΔU = Q − W. It is conservation of energy for heat and work.

cards.front: State the second law in one sentence about heat flow.
cards.back: Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, never the other way, and the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

cards.front: Heat engine efficiency: e = {{W/Q_h}} = 1 − {{Q_c/Q_h}}
cards.back: e = W/Q_h = 1 − Q_c/Q_h. No engine reaches 100%.

cards.front: Carnot (maximum) efficiency: e = 1 − {{T_c/T_h}}, with temperatures in kelvin
cards.back: e = 1 − T_c/T_h. Always use kelvin, never °C.

cards.front: State the third law of thermodynamics.
cards.back: Absolute zero (0 K) cannot be reached in a finite number of steps.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a thermometer scale that ends at 0 K with a wall in front of it labeled 'cannot reach'.

cards.front: Match each law with its big idea.
cards.back: Four laws, four ideas.

cards.front: Convert 27 °C to kelvin.
cards.back: 300 K (add 273 to °C). Kelvin has no negative values.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two thermometers side by side, one in °C and one in K, and mark 0 °C = 273 K.

cards.front: Heat for a temperature change: Q = {{m·c·ΔT}}
cards.back: Q = mcΔT, where c is the specific heat capacity (water: 4186 J/(kg·K)).

cards.front: Heat for a phase change: Q = {{m·L}}
cards.back: Q = mL, and the temperature stays constant while the phase changes.

cards.front: Label this heating curve.
cards.back: temperature T; heat added Q; melting plateau; boiling plateau; liquid warming

cards.front: Order the stages as ice at −10 °C is heated all the way to steam.
cards.back: Ice warms, melts, water warms, boils, steam warms.

cards.front: Match each heat transfer method with its description.
cards.back: Radiation needs no material at all.
pairs: heat carried by a moving fluid

cards.front: Why does the temperature stay flat while ice melts?
cards.back: The added energy breaks bonds between molecules (potential energy) instead of making them move faster.

cards.front: Hot water (m₁, T₁) is mixed with cold water (m₂, T₂) with no losses. How do you find the final temperature?
cards.back: Heat lost = heat gained: m₁c(T₁ − T) = m₂c(T − T₂). Solve for T.

cards.front: Water has c ≈ 4186 J/(kg·K) and cooking oil about 2000. Which warms faster with the same heat?
cards.back: The oil. Lower specific heat means a bigger ΔT for the same Q.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw two pots, one with water and one with oil, with thermometers. Show the oil's thermometer higher.

cards.front: Ideal gas law: PV = {{nRT}}
cards.back: PV = nRT with T in kelvin and R = 8.315 J/(mol·K).

cards.front: Boyle's law (T constant): P₁V₁ = {{P₂V₂}}
cards.back: Squeeze the volume and the pressure goes up in proportion.

cards.front: Charles's law (P constant): V₁/T₁ = {{V₂/T₂}}
cards.back: Use kelvin. Doubling T doubles V.

cards.front: Work done by a gas at constant pressure: W = {{P·ΔV}}
cards.back: W = PΔV. On a P–V diagram it is the area under the curve.

cards.front: Label this P–V diagram.
cards.back: pressure P; volume V; isobaric; isochoric; work = area under curve

cards.front: In an isothermal process of an ideal gas, what are ΔU and Q?
cards.back: ΔU = 0 because T is constant, so Q = W.

cards.front: A bubble rises from deep water to the surface. What happens to its volume?
cards.back: It grows. The pressure drops, so by Boyle's law the volume rises.

cards.front: What is the internal energy of n moles of a monatomic ideal gas?
cards.back: U = (3/2)nRT. It depends only on temperature.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a box of gas atoms with arrows of motion. Write U = (3/2)nRT beside it.

cards.front: Wave speed: v = {{f·λ}}
cards.back: v = fλ. In air at room temperature v ≈ 343 m/s.

cards.front: Label this sound wave.
cards.back: compression; rarefaction; wavelength λ; direction of wave

cards.front: Which sound property sets the pitch, and which sets the loudness?
cards.back: Frequency sets the pitch. Amplitude sets the loudness.

cards.front: How fast is sound in dry air, and does a louder sound travel faster?
cards.back: About 343 m/s. No: loudness does not change the speed. Heat makes it faster, and solids and liquids carry it faster.

cards.front: Echo: distance to the wall d = {{v·t / 2}}
cards.back: The sound goes there and back, so use half of the time.

cards.front: Match each term with its meaning.
cards.back: Sound is a longitudinal wave of pressure.

cards.front: Can sound travel through a vacuum?
cards.back: No. It needs a medium to push on. Light can travel through a vacuum.
cards.sketch_prompt: Draw a bell inside a jar with the air pumped out. Write 'no sound' next to it.

cards.front: Order the media by speed of sound, slowest first.
cards.back: Air, water, steel.
